metadata.title: Against all expectations? What are the differences between resilient and non-resilient schools in the CIL domain

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICILS 2018 microdata for Germany, based on a multi-stage clustered sampling design (random schools, then random students and teachers within schools). Because ICILS achievement is based on a plausible value approach, the authors state that analyses involving CIL achievement were weighted using the student-level weighting factors provided in the dataset to account for unit non-response. For inference, they compute robust standard errors and unbiased significance testing by applying jackknife repeated replication (JRR). The analytic sample is further restricted by excluding schools with fewer than 10 cases and by not imputing missing values on central school-level variables (n=455 missing school-level central variables; n=22 schools with <10 cases), yielding 174 schools and 3,155 students.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Secondary analysis of ICILS 2018 for Germany only. The full ICILS dataset contains 210 schools, 2,328 teachers, and 3,655 students, but the authors restrict to an analytic sample of 174 schools and 3,155 students due to (i) missing data on central school-level variables that were not imputed (n=455) and (ii) exclusion of schools with fewer than 10 cases (n=22). The CIL achievement outcome is based on the ICILS computer-based test with five plausible values per student; analyses are conducted using each plausible value and then averaged/combined according to Rubin’s rules. Multivariate models are estimated with weighted and imputed student-level data and clustered standard errors at the school level (level 2).

main_findings.dataset_used: ICILS 2018 Grade 8 Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) — Germany
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted OLS with jackknife repeated replication (JRR) and clustered schools; R² (Model 1): 0.305; R² (Model 5): 0.411. Key coefficient differences (Type II vs Type I): +65.2 (p<0.001) in M1; +58.8 (p<0.001) in M5. Type IV vs Type I: +89.4 (p<0.001) in M1; +56.4 (p<0.001) in M5.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 Grade 8 Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) data for Germany, the study leveraged school-type classification (resilient vs non-resilient based on HISEI composition and average CIL) together with student, home, and teacher indicators to predict CIL achievement (five plausible values combined via Rubin’s rules), finding that students in resilient low-SES schools (Type II) scored about 65 points higher than students in non-resilient low-SES schools (Type I) even after controlling for all considered factors (about 58.8 points in the fully adjusted model). This indicates that compensatory conditions—especially at the student and parental-home levels—can substantially buffer socioeconomic disadvantage in digital skills, though a residual school-type gap remains and causality cannot be inferred due to cross-sectional design.

data.outcome_summary: The study conducts secondary analyses of ICILS 2018 for Germany, using the Grade 8 computer-based Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) test as the dependent variable. CIL achievement is modeled using five plausible values per student, combined using Rubin’s rules, with student-level weighting factors applied to account for unit non-response and jackknife repeated replication (JRR) used for standard errors. The analytic sample comprises 174 schools and 3,155 students after excluding schools with fewer than 10 cases and not imputing missing values on central school-level variables. The authors estimate weighted OLS regressions with clustered schools (level 2) and stepwise models (student characteristics, home conditions, and school digital conditions). In Model 1, resilient low-SES schools (Type II) show a +65.2 CIL-point advantage over non-resilient low-SES schools (Type I), and in the fully adjusted Model 5 the advantage remains +58.8 points; the overall explanatory power increases from R²=0.305 to R²=0.411. The results are predictive associations rather than causal effects, and the paper does not use machine-learning algorithms for prediction.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is an empirical regression-based study (weighted OLS with plausible values, multiple imputation, and clustered standard errors) rather than a machine-learning predictive modeling paper. Consequently, no ML algorithms are trained or compared, so ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and ml_techniques.primary is left null. The extraction therefore focuses on the ILSA design, plausible value handling, missing-data strategy, and regression-based findings.
